title: Anthropic selects Nasdaq for planned IPO listing
excerpt: The AI company is targeting an October listing and could be valued at $2 trillion, giving Nasdaq another major win after SpaceX
content_html:
Anthropic has chosen Nasdaq as the venue for its planned initial public offering, according to Business Insider, citing a person familiar with the matter. An October debut is the company's current target.

Some estimates have put Anthropic's valuation at $2 trillion, though that figure has not been finalized, according to Business Insider. The company has not yet made its IPO filing public, but it will need to release its financials at least 15 days before beginning its investor road show.

The selection gives Nasdaq a second consecutive high-profile win over the New York Stock Exchange. Nasdaq secured SpaceX's listing earlier this year, with that company valued at $1.75 trillion. The stakes of that rivalry have risen sharply, driven by the outsized value of these deals and a prolonged drought in significant tech market debuts, according to Business Insider.

Membership in the Nasdaq-100 Index requires that a company's shares trade on the Nasdaq exchange, according to Business Insider. Nasdaq cut its minimum seasoning period to 15 trading days for qualifying IPOs after SpaceX's inclusion in the index — a rule that made the exchange more attractive to large listings seeking index inclusion.

Anthropic is moving toward a public market debut at a moment when AI safety concerns are drawing wider attention. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said his company would not go public given the current controversy surrounding existential threats from AI, according to Business Insider. That debate intensified last week after a former Anthropic employee posted on social media a warning of a greater than 10% human extinction risk from AI, according to Business Insider.

On the mechanics of where a company lists, the choice of exchange has little definitive effect on how a stock ultimately trades, according to Business Insider. A notable distinction is that the two exchanges handle first-day price discovery differently, and when IPO volume is heavy the process can break down, as it did for Nasdaq when Facebook went public in 2012, according to Business Insider.
